source.title: Sparse autoencoders reveal selective remapping of visual concepts during adaptation
source.authors: Hyesu Lim; Jin-Ho Choi; Jaegul Choo; Steffen Schneider

record.file_problem: The full paper, including appendices, is present. Some figures and tables are flattened in the text extraction, but the relevant prose and reported numerical results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses polysemanticity and sparse autoencoders, but its experiments analyze SAE latents in CLIP rather than neuron poles or the claim versions’ specified tests. It does not test the neuron-pole audit claim.
record.gate_note: The study trains and interprets PatchSAE latents, then masks those latents to study CLIP classification and adaptation. These latents are not the model’s own neurons or neuron poles, and the paper does not test explanations on held-out activations or score neuron explanations. The SAE-latent masking results below are related findings, not tests of a listed version.
record.test_reason: The study trains a sparse autoencoder (PatchSAE) on CLIP ViT-B/16 residual-stream activations and analyses SAE latents: qualitative interpretability, masking effects on classification, and adaptation remapping. It never audits individual neurons or neuron poles, never tests the InceptionV1 examples, never builds neuron-based attribution graphs, and never scores explanations on held-out activations. Its related-work section restates the standard polysemanticity and superposition framing without testing it. No listed version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that prompt-based adaptation (MaPLe) mostly reuses concepts already present in CLIP's SAE latents and remaps them to downstream classes. Only EuroSAT, which has a larger distribution shift, shows a non-negligible number of concepts suppressed or newly activated.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses a PatchSAE trained on CLIP vision-transformer activations, then studies SAE-latent interpretation and masking. It does not use the neuron-pole audit or held-out explanation tests described in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The classification results vary with SAE-latent selection (per-class versus random or dataset-level), the number of masked latents, classification backbone, and task dataset. The paper also reports differences across SAE hook layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Masking per-class top-activating PatchSAE latents in CLIP ViT-B/16 strongly changes ImageNet zero-shot accuracy. Random or dataset-level latent selections have marginal effect until many latents are masked. The identity mask gives 64.82% vs 68.25% for the original model, and the all-zero mask gives 0.1%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE latents (not neurons) in CLIP's vision encoder carry class-discriminative information, as shown by masking effects on classification.

fits_no_version.finding: The study reports qualitatively that many rarely-activated, high-label-entropy SAE latents are uninterpretable, while frequent, high-activation latents are more interpretable. No shares are quantified.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Interpretability of SAE latents in CLIP varies with activation frequency and strength; this concerns SAE latents, not neurons.

record.problems: The study analyzes SAE latents rather than individual neurons or neuron poles, and provides no held-out tests or automated scores of neuron explanations. Interpretability is assessed mainly through qualitative inspection. The main SAE is trained on CLIP ViT-B/16 at the 11th layer; the authors state that analysis of other vision encoders and full fine-tuning are future work.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows were included for the other datasets, base/novel splits, or MaPLe masking combinations: those results concern SAE-latent masking and adaptation performance, not neuron poles or a claim version. Figures 5(c), 6, and 11 and Table 1 report further task- and backbone-specific results.

untested.parts: Shares across language models, MoE models and scale.
Reinterpretation of the InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron as pose detection (recursive generalization).
Effect of architecture, regularization and tools on the share of interpretable neurons in vision models.
Attribution graphs built from a model's own neurons without a replacement model.
Whether explanations drawn from activating examples predict where neurons fire on new inputs.
Simulation-based automated scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The neuron/SAE distinction is decisive: all quantitative results concern SAE latents, so no row bears on any version. Interpretability of latents is assessed qualitatively, from reference images and statistics.

versions.untested_parts: Neuron-pole job counts and the share of poles with one job, two related jobs, or no understood job.
Neuron-pole interpretability across language models, dense and mixture-of-experts models, and model scale.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose detection, and recursive generalization versus superposition.
Architecture, regularization, and tools as explanations for neuron interpretability, including the InceptionV1-sized vision-model estimates.
Attribution graphs built from a large model’s own neurons and whether they explain behavior without a replacement model and its reconstruction error.
Whether explanations based on activating examples predict where neurons fire on unseen activations.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

rows.subject: CLIP ViT-B/16
rows.operation_detail: Replaced the intermediate representation with SAE reconstruction using the identity mask (all SAE latents active).
rows.note: The paper describes this as recovering the original classification performance with small reconstruction errors; this is an SAE-latent result, not a neuron-pole test.
rows.check: SAE reconstruction fidelity (64.82% vs 68.25%). This is a check on the study's own tool, not a measure of neuron interpretability. The state 'observed' has no version to refer to.

rows.subject: CLIP ViT-B/16
rows.operation_detail: Replaced the intermediate representation with SAE reconstruction after masking all SAE latents off.
rows.note: The paper says the all-zero mask removes relevant information. This concerns SAE latents, not neuron poles.
rows.check: The all-zero mask is a trivial sanity check on the SAE method and bears on no version.
